To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Weber Ratio is smaller and the Constant Error is smaller when the standard and comparison stimuli are presented simultaneously than when they are presented successively; (2) the Weber Ratio and Constant Error are smaller with the preferred hand than with the non-preferred hand; (3) the Weber Ratio with the preferred hand is larger and the Constant Error with the non-prefered hand is smaller when the comparison stimulus is presented before the standard stimulus than when the standard stimulus is presented before.

(1) simultaneous presentation of the weights to be discriminated results in poorer discrimination than successive presentation, (2) the poorer discrimination is due to the fact that the simultaneous presentation results in greater variability in the responses of the sensory neurons, (3) the variability is due to the greater number of neurons activated by the simultaneous presentation, and (4) the number of neurons activated is greater in simultaneous presentation than in successive because of the larger receptive fields of the neurons in the simultaneous condition.

1) the simultaneous presentation of two stimuli in the tactile modality produces less accurate discrimination than the successive presentation of two stimuli; 2) the simultaneous presentation condition produces more variable constant errors than does the successive presentation condition; 3) the simultaneous presentation produces a greater Weber fraction than does the successive; and 4) the simultaneous presentation conditions produce more variable constant errors and greater Weber fractions than does the successive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a problem of considerable importance to psychologists, namely, the question of the relationship of perception and action.
the problem of the relationship between the physical and perceptual properties of stimuli and their psychological effects.
the effects of stimulus presentation mode and hand of presentation on the accuracy of tactile weight discrimination.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results obtained in this study are not consistent with a theory of tactile discrimination based on the assumption of a single, homogeneous tactile system.
the tactile system is more sensitive to the successive presentation of stimuli.
simultaneous interhand judgments produce more variable constant errors than do successive intrahand judgments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the tactile system is organized in a manner that is similar to that found in the visual system, but that the tactile system has a greater capacity for processing simultaneous information than does the visual system.
the tactile system, unlike the visual system, does not have a single, central mechanism for processing information from the two hands.
the tactile system is organized so as to facilitate the detection of changes in the intensity of a stimulus rather than its localization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated a method for the production of a large number of high quality, high resolution images of the human hand in a short period of time.
the simultaneous presentation of the two stimuli in the tactile modality results in poorer performance.
the simultaneous presentation of two stimuli is less sensitive to differences between the stimuli than is the successive presentation.
